confirmed: Read the entire local markdown conversion, including Supplementary table 1 and references, and independently extracted all 11 PDF pages. The document is the preprint titled Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays., by Željana Bašić, Ana Banovac, Ivana Kružić, and Ivan Jerković; it is not the journal version of record (PDF p. 1; complete PDF pp. 1–11).

The source.version qualification is supported: the local PDF has no printed arXiv version marker, so v1 versus v2 is not established from it. The arXiv submission history independently confirms v1 on 2023-02-09 and v2 on 2023-10-31, each listed as 344 KB (https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04536, submission history).

Crossref independently confirms the journal title ChatGPT-3.5 as writing assistance in students’ essays, Humanities and Social Sciences Communications volume 10, article 750, publication date 2023-10-28, and abstract arm sizes n = 9 and n = 9 (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1057/s41599-023-02269-7). Only journal metadata and abstract were read; the publisher PDF URL returned a Client Challenge, so no journal full-text claim is made.

There is one original people study, not a synthesis or an AI-only comparison. The authors balanced the two groups on study module and GPA but do not state random assignment anywhere in the full preprint; quasi_people, randomized = not_stated, criterion_1 = unclear, and randomized counts = null are appropriately cautious (PDF pp. 2–3, Materials and methods; full PDF pp. 1–11).

The sample comprises 18 volunteer students out of 50 course enrollees, with 9 in each arm; 50 is the course enrollment, not the analyzed sample size. No participant exclusions are reported, and the table includes Control1–Control9 and GPT1–GPT9; n_analyzed = 18 and criterion_2 = not_met are supported, while no randomized participant count is provided (PDF p. 1, Abstract; pp. 2–3, Materials and methods; p. 6, Supplementary table 1).

Participants were second-year master’s students in forensic sciences at the University of Split, Croatia. Control GPA was 3.92 ± 0.46 and experimental GPA was 3.92 ± 0.57; the experimental group used what the preprint calls ChatGTP assistance, version 2.1.0 (PDF pp. 2–3, Materials and methods).

The task was an 800–1000-word Croatian essay on advantages and disadvantages of biometric identification in forensic sciences, using Vancouver citations, with four hours allowed. The experimental group was introduced to ChatGPT and the control group was supervised to prevent its use (PDF p. 3, Materials and methods).

Two teachers graded mechanics, style, content, and format, resolving disagreements by consensus; grades were converted as A=4, B=3, C=2, D=1 and averaged across the four elements. This supports the essay-quality outcome, without establishing a direct creativity rating (PDF p. 3, Materials and methods).

S1-O1.reported and the one-line essay-score values match: control 2.39 ± 0.71 versus GPT 2.00 ± 0.73; regression group P = 0.184. The regression included group, writing duration, module, and GPA; no statistically significant group association was reported (PDF p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Results; Figure 1 caption on p. 5).
The recorded writing durations match: GPT 172.22 ± 31.59 minutes and control 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes (PDF p. 4, Results).

S1-O3.reported matches exactly: text unauthenticity 11.87% ±13.45 in the GPT-assisted group and 9.96% ± 9.81% in the control group. No inferential between-arm test of this outcome is reported; treatment_higher describes the printed means only (PDF p. 4, Results).

S1-O2.reported and the one-line Jaccard values match the pooled Results summary: median 0.002 (0 – 0.054). Supplementary table 1 lists pairwise values, including a displayed maximum of 0.0537 at Control1–Control4, consistent with the rounded upper endpoint in the prose; it provides no arm-level similarity summary or test (PDF p. 4, Results; p. 6, Supplementary table 1, independently recovered with find_tables).

The discussion describes no remarkable pairwise essay similarities regardless of ChatGPT use, but does not provide an arm-level contrast. The one-line finding correctly states that no arm-level similarity contrast was reported (PDF p. 7, Discussion; p. 4, Results).
The synthesis fields are correctly left empty: this is one empirical study and reports no meta-analytic study count, pooled estimate, or standardizer (PDF pp. 2–4, Materials and methods and Results).
summary: The preprint reports 18 students (9 per group), does not state random assignment, and its numerical results match the form. Seven corrections concern observational context, the output-diversity criterion, the included supplement, and the diversity, statistics, and quotation fields.
